{{short description|Group of unitary matrices}}
{{redirect|U(2)|other topics|U2 (disambiguation)}}
{{Group theory sidebar |Topological}}
{{Lie groups |Classical}}

In [[mathematics]], the '''unitary group''' of degree <math>n</math>, denoted <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math>, is the [[group (mathematics)|group]] of <math>n\times n</math> [[Unitary matrix|unitary matrices]], with the group operation of [[matrix multiplication]]. The unitary group is a [[subgroup]] of the [[general linear group]] <math>\operatorname{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})</math>, and it has as a subgroup the [[special unitary group]], consisting of those unitary matrices with [[determinant]] <math>1</math>.

In the simple case <math>n=1</math>, the group <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math> corresponds to the [[circle group]], isomorphic to the set of all [[complex number]]s that have [[Absolute_value#Complex_numbers|absolute value]] <math>1</math>, under multiplication. All the unitary groups contain copies of this group.

The unitary group <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> is a [[real number|real]] [[Lie group]] of dimension <math>n^2</math>. The [[Lie algebra]] of <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> consists of <math>n\times n</math> [[skew-Hermitian matrix|skew-Hermitian matrices]], with the [[Lie algebra|Lie bracket]] given by the [[commutator]].

The '''general unitary group''', also called the '''group of unitary similitudes''', consists of all [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] <math>A</math> such that <math>A^*A</math> is a nonzero multiple of the [[identity matrix]], and is just the product of the unitary group with the group of all positive multiples of the identity matrix.

Unitary groups may also be defined over fields other than the complex numbers.  The '''hyperorthogonal group''' is an archaic name for the unitary group, especially over [[finite field]]s.

== Properties ==
Since the [[determinant]] of a unitary matrix is a complex number with norm <math>1</math>, the determinant gives a [[group homomorphism]]
<math display="block">\det \colon \operatorname{U}(n) \to \operatorname{U}(1).</math>

The [[kernel (group theory)|kernel]] of this homomorphism is the set of unitary matrices with determinant <math>1</math>. This subgroup is called the [[special unitary group]], denoted <math>\operatorname{SU}(n)</math>. We then have a [[short exact sequence]] of Lie groups:
<math display="block">1 \to \operatorname{SU}(n) \to \operatorname{U}(n) \to \operatorname{U}(1) \to 1.</math>

The above map <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> to <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math> has a section: we can view <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math> as the subgroup of <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> that are diagonal with <math>e^{i\theta}</math> in the upper left corner and <math>1</math> on the rest of the diagonal. Therefore <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> is a [[semidirect product]] of <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math> with <math>\operatorname{SU}(n)</math>.

The unitary group <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> is not [[abelian group|abelian]] for <math>n>1</math>. The [[center of a group|center]] of <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> is the set of scalar matrices <math>\lambda I</math> with <math>\lambda\in\operatorname{U}(1)</math>; this follows from [[Schur's lemma]]. The center is then isomorphic to <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math>. Since the center of <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> is a <math>1</math>-dimensional abelian [[normal subgroup]] of <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math>, the unitary group is not [[Semisimple algebraic group|semisimple]], but it is [[Reductive group|reductive]].

== Topology ==
The unitary group <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> is endowed with the [[relative topology]] as a subset of <math>M(n,\mathbb{C})</math>, the set of all <math>n\times n</math> complex matrices, which is itself homeomorphic to a <math>2n^2</math>-dimensional [[Euclidean space]].

As a topological space, <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> is both [[compact space|compact]] and [[connected space|connected]]. To show that <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> is connected, recall that any unitary matrix <math>A</math> can be [[diagonalized]] by another unitary matrix <math>S</math>. Any diagonal unitary matrix must have complex numbers of absolute value <math>1</math> on the [[main diagonal]]. We can therefore write
<math display="block">A = S\,\operatorname{diag}\left(e^{i\theta_1}, \dots, e^{i\theta_n}\right)\,S^{-1}.</math>

A [[path (topology)|path]] in <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> from the identity to <math>A</math> is then given by
<math display="block">t \mapsto S \, \operatorname{diag}\left(e^{it\theta_1}, \dots, e^{it\theta_n}\right)\,S^{-1} .</math>

The unitary group is not [[simply connected]]; the fundamental group of <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> is infinite cyclic for all <math>n</math>:<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Proposition 13.11</ref>
<math display="block">\pi_1(\operatorname{U}(n))\cong\mathbb{Z}.</math>

To see this, note that the above splitting of <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> as a [[semidirect product]] of <math>\operatorname{SU}(n)</math> and <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math> induces a topological product structure on <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math>, so that
<math display="block">\pi_1(\operatorname{U}(n)) \cong \pi_1(\operatorname{SU}(n)) \times \pi_1(\operatorname{U}(1)).</math>

Now the first unitary group <math>\operatorname{U}(1)</math> is topologically a [[circle]], which is well known to have a [[fundamental group]] isomorphic to <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>, whereas <math>\operatorname{SU}(n)</math> is simply connected.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Proposition 13.11</ref>

The determinant map <math>\det\colon\operatorname{U}(n)\rightarrow\operatorname{U}(1)</math> induces an isomorphism of fundamental groups, with the splitting <math>\operatorname{U}(1)\rightarrow\operatorname{U}(n)</math> inducing the inverse.

The [[Weyl group]] of <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> is the [[symmetric group]] <math>S_n</math>, acting on the diagonal torus  by permuting the entries:
<math display="block">\operatorname{diag}\left(e^{i\theta_1}, \dots, e^{i\theta_n}\right) \mapsto \operatorname{diag}\left(e^{i\theta_{\sigma(1)}}, \dots, e^{i\theta_{\sigma(n)}}\right)</math>

== Related groups ==

=== 2-out-of-3 property ===
The unitary group is the 3-fold intersection of the [[orthogonal group|orthogonal]], [[linear complex structure|complex]], and [[symplectic group|symplectic]] groups:
<math display="block">\operatorname{U}(n)=\operatorname{O}(2n)\cap\operatorname{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})\cap\operatorname{Sp}(2n, \mathbb{R}).</math>

Thus a unitary structure can be seen as an orthogonal structure, a complex structure, and a symplectic structure, which are required to be ''compatible'' (meaning that one uses the same <math>J</math> in the complex structure and the symplectic form, and that this <math>J</math> is orthogonal; writing all the groups as matrix groups fixes a <math>J</math> (which is orthogonal) and ensures compatibility).

In fact, it is the intersection of any ''two'' of these three; thus a compatible orthogonal and complex structure induce a symplectic structure, and so forth.<ref>{{cite book |last=Arnold |first=V.I. |author-link1=Vladimir Arnold |title=Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics |url=https://archive.org/details/mathematicalmeth00arno_565 |url-access=limited |publisher=Springer |edition=Second |year=1989 |page=[https://archive.org/details/mathematicalmeth00arno_565/page/n238 225]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/symplectic.html |title=Symplectic, Quaternionic, Fermionic |last=Baez |first=John |access-date=1 February 2012}}</ref>

At the level of equations, this can be seen as follows:
{| class="wikitable"
|-
! Structure !! Equation
|-
| Symplectic || <math>A^\mathsf{T}JA = J</math>
|-
| Complex || <math>A^{-1}JA = J</math>
|-
| Orthogonal || <math>A^\mathsf{T} = A^{-1}</math>
|}

Any two of these equations implies the third.

At the level of forms, this can be seen by decomposing a Hermitian form into its real and imaginary parts: the real part is symmetric (orthogonal), and the imaginary part is skew-symmetric (symplectic)—and these are related by the complex structure (which is the compatibility). On an [[almost Kähler manifold]], one can write this decomposition as <math>h=g+i\omega</math>, where <math>h</math> is the Hermitian form, <math>g</math> is the [[Riemannian metric]], <math>i</math> is the [[almost complex manifold|almost complex structure]], and <math>\omega</math> is the [[almost symplectic manifold|almost symplectic structure]].

From the point of view of [[Lie group]]s, this can partly be explained as follows: <math>\operatorname{O}(2n)</math> is the [[maximal compact subgroup]] of <math>\operatorname{GL}(2n,\mathbb{R})</math>, and <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> is the maximal compact subgroup of both <math>\operatorname{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})</math> and <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n)</math>. Thus the intersection <math>\operatorname{O}(2n)\cap\operatorname{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})</math> or <math>\operatorname{O}(2n)\cap\operatorname{Sp}(2n)</math> is the maximal compact subgroup of both of these, so <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math>. From this perspective, what is unexpected is the intersection <math>\operatorname{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})\cap\operatorname{Sp}(2n)=\operatorname{U}(n)</math>.

=== Special unitary and projective unitary groups ===
[[File:PSU-PU-2.svg|400px|right]]
{{see also|Special unitary group|Projective unitary group}}

Just as the orthogonal group <math>\operatorname{O}(n)</math> has the [[special orthogonal group]] <math>\operatorname{SO}(n)</math> as subgroup and the [[projective orthogonal group]] <math>\operatorname{PO}(n)</math> as quotient, and the [[projective special orthogonal group]] <math>\operatorname{PSO}(n)</math> as [[subquotient]], the unitary group <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> has associated to it the [[special unitary group]] <math>\operatorname{SU}(n)</math>, the [[projective unitary group]] <math>\operatorname{PU}(n)</math>, and the [[projective special unitary group]] <math>\operatorname{PSU}(n)</math>. These are related as by the [[commutative diagram]] (with [[exact sequence|exact]] rows and columns) on the right; notably, both projective groups are equal: <math>\operatorname{PSU}(n)=\operatorname{PU}(n)</math>.

The above is for the classical unitary group (over the complex numbers) – for [[#Finite_fields|unitary groups over finite fields]], one similarly obtains special unitary and projective unitary groups, but in general <math>\operatorname{PSU}(n,q^2)\neq\operatorname{PU}(n,q^2)</math>.

== G-structure: almost Hermitian ==
In the language of [[G-structure|''G''-structure]]s, a manifold with a <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math>-structure is an [[almost Hermitian manifold]].

== Generalizations ==
From the point of view of [[Lie theory]], the classical unitary group is a real form of the [[Steinberg group (Lie theory)|Steinberg group]] <math>{}^2\!A_n</math>, which is an [[algebraic group]] that arises from the combination of the ''diagram automorphism'' of the general linear group (reversing the [[Dynkin diagram]] <math>A_n</math>, which corresponds to transpose inverse) and the ''[[field automorphism]]'' of the extension <math>\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{R}</math> (namely [[complex conjugation]]). Both these automorphisms are automorphisms of the algebraic group, have order <math>2</math>, and commute, and the unitary group is the fixed points of the product automorphism, as an algebraic group. The classical unitary group is a real form of this group, corresponding to the standard [[Hermitian form]] <math>\Psi</math>, which is positive definite.

This can be generalized in a number of ways:
* generalizing to other Hermitian forms yields indefinite unitary groups <math>\operatorname{U}(p,q)</math>;
* the field extension can be replaced by any degree <math>2</math> separable algebra, most notably a degree <math>2</math> extension of a finite field;
* generalizing to other diagrams yields other [[groups of Lie type]], namely the other [[Steinberg group (Lie theory)|Steinberg groups]] <math>{}^2\!D_n</math>, <math>{}^2\!E_6</math>, <math>{}^3\!D_4</math>, (in addition to <math>{}^2\!A_n</math>) and [[Suzuki–Ree group]]s
*: <math>{}^2\!B_2\left(2^{2n+1}\right), {}^2\!F_4\left(2^{2n+1}\right), {}^2\!G_2\left(3^{2n+1}\right)</math>;
* considering a generalized unitary group as an algebraic group, one can take its points over various algebras.

=== Indefinite forms ===
Analogous to the [[indefinite orthogonal group]]s, one can define an '''indefinite unitary group''', by considering the transforms that preserve a given Hermitian form, not necessarily positive definite (but generally taken to be non-degenerate). Here one is working with a [[vector space]] over the complex numbers.

Given a Hermitian form <math>\Psi</math> on a complex vector space <math>V</math>, the unitary group <math>\operatorname{U}(\Psi)</math> is the group of transforms that preserve the form: the transform <math>M</math> such that <math>\Psi(Mv,Mw)=\Psi(v,w)</math> for all <math>v,w\in V</math>. In terms of matrices, representing the form by a matrix denoted <math>\Phi</math>, this says that <math>M^*\Phi M=\Phi</math>.

Just as for [[Symmetric bilinear form|symmetric forms]] over the reals, Hermitian forms are determined by [[Signature of a quadratic form|signature]], and are all [[Matrix congruence|unitarily congruent]] to a diagonal form with <math>p</math> entries of <math>1</math> on the diagonal and <math>q</math> entries of <math>-1</math>. The non-degenerate assumption is equivalent to <math>p+q=n</math>. In a standard basis, this is represented as a quadratic form as:
<math display="block">\lVert z \rVert_\Psi^2 = \lVert z_1 \rVert^2 + \dots + \lVert z_p \rVert^2 - \lVert z_{p+1} \rVert^2 - \dots - \lVert z_n \rVert^2,</math>

and as a symmetric form as:
<math display="block">\Psi(w, z) = \bar w_1 z_1 + \cdots + \bar w_p z_p - \bar w_{p+1}z_{p+1} - \cdots - \bar w_n z_n.</math>

The resulting group is denoted <math>\operatorname{U}(p,q)</math>.

=== Finite fields ===
Over the [[finite field]] with <math>q=p^r</math> elements, <math>\mathbb{F}_q</math>, there is a unique quadratic extension field, <math>\mathbb{F}_{q^2}</math>, with order <math>2</math> automorphism <math>\alpha\colon x \mapsto x^q</math> (the <math>r</math>th power of the [[Frobenius automorphism]]). This allows one to define a Hermitian form on an <math>\mathbb{F}_{q^2}</math> vector space <math>V</math>, as an <math>\mathbb{F}_q</math>-bilinear map <math>\Psi\colon V \times V \to K</math> such that <math>\Psi(w, v) = \alpha \left(\Psi(v, w)\right)</math> and <math>\Psi(w, cv) = c\Psi(w, v)</math> for <math>c\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}</math>.{{clarify|What is K?|date=June 2014}} Further, all non-degenerate Hermitian forms on a vector space over a finite field<!-- clear from context, but I think it fails infinite fields of pos char--> are unitarily congruent to the standard one, represented by the identity matrix; that is, any Hermitian form is unitarily equivalent to
<math display="block">\Psi(w, v) = w^\alpha \cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^q v_i</math>
where <math>w_i,v_i</math> represent the coordinates of <math>w,v\in V</math> in some particular <math>\mathbb{F}_{q^2}</math>-basis of the <math>n</math>-dimensional space <math>V</math>.{{sfnp|Grove|2002|loc=Theorem 10.3}}

Thus one can define a (unique) unitary group of dimension <math>n</math> for the extension <math>\mathbb{F}_{q^2}/\mathbb{F}_q</math>, denoted either as <math>\operatorname{U}(n,q)</math> or <math>\operatorname{U}(n,q^2)</math> depending on the author. The subgroup of the unitary group consisting of matrices of determinant <math>1</math> is called the '''special unitary group''' and denoted <math>\operatorname{SU}(n,q)</math> or <math>\operatorname{SU}(n,q^2)</math>. For convenience, this article will use the <math>\operatorname{U}(n,q^2)</math> convention. The center of <math>\operatorname{U}(n,q^2)</math> has order <math>q+1</math> and consists of the scalar matrices that are unitary, that is those matrices <math>cI_V</math> with <math>c^{q+1}=1</math>. The center of the special unitary group has order <math>\gcd(n,q+1)</math> and consists of those unitary scalars which also have order dividing <math>n</math>. The quotient of the unitary group by its center is called the '''[[projective unitary group]]''', <math>\operatorname{PU}(n,q^2)</math>, and the quotient of the special unitary group by its center is the '''[[projective special unitary group]]''' <math>\operatorname{PSU}(n,q^2)</math>. In most cases (<math>n>1</math> and <math>(n,q^2)\not\in\{(2,2^2),(2,3^2),(3,2^2)\}</math>), <math>\operatorname{SU}(n,q^2)</math> is a [[perfect group]] and <math>\operatorname{PSU}(n,q^2)</math> is a finite [[simple group]].{{sfnp|Grove|2002|loc=Theorems 11.22 and 11.26}}

=== Degree-2 separable algebras ===
More generally, given a field <math>k</math> and a degree-<math>2</math> separable <math>k</math>-algebra <math>K</math> (which may be a field extension but need not be), one can define unitary groups with respect to this extension.

First, there is a unique <math>k</math>-automorphism of <math>K</math> <math>a\mapsto\bar{a}</math> which is an involution and fixes exactly <math>k</math> (<math>a = \bar{a}</math> if and only if <math>a\in k</math>).<ref>Milne, [http://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/aag.html Algebraic Groups and Arithmetic Groups], p. 103</ref> This generalizes complex conjugation and the conjugation of degree <math>2</math> finite field extensions, and allows one to define Hermitian forms and unitary groups as above.

=== Algebraic groups ===
The equations defining a unitary group are polynomial equations over <math>k</math> (but not over <math>K</math>): for the standard form <math>\Phi=I</math>, the equations are given in matrices as <math>A^*A=I</math>, where <math>A^* = \bar{A}^\mathsf{T}</math> is the [[conjugate transpose]]. Given a different form, they are <math>A^*\Phi A=\Phi</math>. The unitary group is thus an [[algebraic group]], whose points over a <math>k</math>-algebra <math>R</math> are given by:
<math display="block">\operatorname{U}(n, K/k, \Phi)(R) := \left\{ A \in \operatorname{GL}(n, K \otimes_k R) : A^*\Phi A = \Phi\right\}.</math>

For the field extension <math>\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{R}</math> and the standard (positive definite) Hermitian form, these yield an algebraic group with real and complex points given by:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \operatorname{U}(n,\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{R})(\mathbb{R}) &= \operatorname{U}(n) \\
  \operatorname{U}(n,\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{R})(\mathbb{C}) &= \operatorname{GL}(n,\mathbb{C}).
\end{align}</math>

In fact, the unitary group is a [[linear algebraic group]].

==== Unitary group of a quadratic module ====
The unitary group of a quadratic module is a generalisation of the linear algebraic group <math>U</math> just defined, which incorporates as special cases many different [[Classical group|classical algebraic groups]]. The definition goes back to Anthony Bak's thesis.<ref>{{cite conference |first=Anthony |last=Bak |year=1969 |chapter=On modules with quadratic forms |title=Algebraic K-Theory and its Geometric Applications |editor-first1=Robert M. F. |editor-last1=Moss |editor-first2=Charles B. |editor-last2=Thomas |series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics |volume=108 |pages=55-66 |publisher=Springer |doi=10.1007/BFb0059990 |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/BFb0059986|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

To define it, one has to define quadratic modules first:

Let <math>R</math> be a ring with anti-automorphism <math>J</math>, <math>\varepsilon\in R^\times</math> such that <math>r^{J^2} = \varepsilon r \varepsilon^{-1}</math> for all <math>r</math> in <math>R</math> and <math>\varepsilon^J = \varepsilon^{-1}</math>. Define
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \Lambda_{\min} & :=\left\{r\in R:r-r^J\varepsilon\right\}, \\
  \Lambda_{\max} & :=\left\{r\in R:r^J\varepsilon=-r\right\}.
\end{align}</math>

Let <math>\Lambda\subseteq R</math> be an additive subgroup of <math>R</math>, then <math>\Lambda</math> is called ''form parameter'' if <math>\Lambda_{\min}\subseteq\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda_{\max}</math> and <math>r^J\Lambda r\subseteq\Lambda</math>. A pair <math>(R,\Lambda)</math> such that <math>R</math> is a ring and <math>\Lambda</math> a form parameter is called ''form ring''.

Let <math>M</math> be an <math>R</math>-module and <math>f</math> a <math>J</math>-sesquilinear form on <math>M</math> (i.e., <math>f(xr, ys) = r^J f(x, y)s</math> for any <math>x,y\in M</math> and <math>r,s\in R</math>). Define <math>h(x,y):=f(x,y)+f(y,x)^J\varepsilon\in R</math> and <math>q(x):=f(x,x)\in R/\Lambda</math>, then <math>f</math> is said to ''define'' the ''<math>\Lambda</math>-quadratic form'' <math>(h,q)</math> on <math>M</math>. A ''quadratic module'' over <math>(R,\Lambda)</math> is a triple <math>(M,h,q)</math> such that <math>M</math> is an <math>R</math>-module and <math>(h,q)</math> is a <math>\Lambda</math>-quadratic form.

To any quadratic module <math>(M,h,q)</math> defined by a <math>J</math>-sesquilinear form <math>f</math> on <math>M</math> over a form ring <math>(R,\Lambda)</math> one can associate the ''unitary group''
<math display="block">U(M):=\{\sigma\in\operatorname{GL}(M):\forall x,y\in M,h(\sigma x,\sigma y)=h(x,y)\text{ and }q(\sigma x)=q(x)\}.</math>

The special case where <math>\Lambda=\Lambda_{\max}</math>, with <math>J</math> any non-trivial involution (i.e., <math>J\neq\operatorname{id}_R</math>, <math>J^2=\operatorname{id}_R</math> and <math>\varepsilon=-1</math> gives back the "classical" unitary group (as an algebraic group).

== Polynomial invariants ==
The unitary groups are the automorphisms of two polynomials in real non-commutative variables:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  C_1 &= \left(u^2 + v^2\right) + \left(w^2 + x^2\right) + \left(y^2 + z^2\right) + \ldots \\
  C_2 &= \left(uv - vu\right) + \left(wx - xw\right) + \left(yz - zy\right) + \ldots
\end{align}</math>

These are easily seen to be the real and imaginary parts of the complex form <math>Z \overline{Z}</math>. The two invariants separately are invariants of <math>\operatorname{O}(2n)</math> and <math>\operatorname{Sp}(2n)</math>. Combined they make the invariants of <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> which is a subgroup of both these groups. The variables must be non-commutative in these invariants otherwise the second polynomial is identically zero.
